artiest/eddie-van-halen.text:
Eddie Van Halen was born on 26 January 1955 in Amsterdam and grew up in Nijmegen. His father was a jazz musician, his mother came from Java. In 1962 the family emigrated to Pasadena, California. Eddie and his older brother Alex had piano lessons, but became captivated by British bands such as The Beatles. Eddie began on drums, left those to Alex and switched to electric guitar. Eric Clapton was his great example.

In 1972 the brothers formed the band Mammoth. When the singer David Lee Roth joined, the name became Van Halen in 1974. The debut album Van Halen (1978) became one of the most successful debuts in rock. On 1984, that year's album, Eddie played a synthesizer riff in Jump, and it became the band's only number 1 on the American pop chart. Outside his own band he played the guitar solo on Michael Jackson's Beat It in 1982. In doing so he also adjusted the structure of the song and refused to be paid for it.

Van Halen popularised the tapping technique, in which the guitarist plays on the neck with both hands and so creates lightning-fast arpeggios. He often built his guitars himself from separate parts, such as the red, white and black striped Frankenstrat. He is regarded as one of the greatest guitarists in rock history. In 2007 the band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Eddie Van Halen died on 6 October 2020 in Santa Monica, aged 65.
artiest/eddie-van-halen.listen: Listen to Jump (1984). The song begins not with guitar but with a synthesizer riff that Eddie Van Halen plays himself. Notice the moment when the guitar still comes to the fore in the solo.

artiest/edgar-froese.text:
Edgar Froese was a German musician and pioneer of electronic music, born in 1944 in Tilsit in East Prussia. After the war his mother settled in Berlin with the rest of the family. He had piano lessons from the age of twelve and began on guitar at fifteen. Among other things he worked as a designer of advertising posters for the Berlin buses and studied psychology and philosophy in the evenings. In 1965 he founded the band The Ones, which played psychedelic rock. During a stay in Spain the group was invited to Salvador Dalí's villa in Cadaqués, a meeting that spurred him towards more experimental work.

After The Ones disbanded in 1967, Froese looked in Berlin for musicians for a free rock group, which became Tangerine Dream. He was the only member to experience the whole history of the group, until his death. He also made solo albums, such as Aqua from 1974, Epsilon in Malaysian Pale from 1975, Macula Transfer from 1976, Stuntman from 1979 and Dalinetopia from 2004. David Bowie said that Epsilon in Malaysian Pale had a great influence on him and was the soundtrack of his life in Berlin. Froese was friends with Bowie, Brian Eno and Iggy Pop, and Pop and Bowie lived for a time at his home in Schöneberg.

Froese stood for a music of long, floating sounds, made with synthesizers, within the German experiment of the 1970s. His son Jerome played in Tangerine Dream from 1990 to 2006. Froese died in Vienna in 2015.
artiest/edgar-froese.listen: Listen to Epsilon in Malaysian Pale and notice the slow, broad sounds of the electronic instruments. Can you hear how the piece stretches out instead of becoming a clear song?

artiest/edgard-varese.text:
Edgard Varèse was born in Paris in 1883 and grew up with relatives in Burgundy. His father, an engineer, wanted him to study engineering, but Edgard chose music. He studied in Paris at the Schola Cantorum and the conservatoire and in 1907 moved to Berlin, where the progressive composer Ferruccio Busoni strongly influenced him. Almost all of his early work was lost or destroyed by him. In 1915 he left for the United States, where he started again.

In New York he wrote Amériques, which was performed in 1926 by the Philadelphia Orchestra under Leopold Stokowski. Pieces such as Hyperprism, Octandre and Intégrales followed, mainly for winds and percussion. Around 1930 he wrote Ionisation, for percussion and sirens, one of the first Western works for percussion instruments alone. Varèse dreamed early on of electronic sounds. Ecuatorial uses two theremins, and in Déserts (1954) an orchestra alternates with a tape. For the Philips Pavilion at Expo 58 in Brussels he made the Poème électronique.

Varèse did not think in melodies and chords, but in timbre, rhythm and blocks of sound. He called his music organised sound and asked what music was, if not organised noise. His entire surviving output lasts only about three hours, yet many composers of the late twentieth century named him as an example. Because of his work with new instruments and electronics he gained the nickname father of electronic music. He died in New York in 1965.
artiest/edgard-varese.listen: Listen to the Poème électronique and notice the sounds: many of them do not come from ordinary instruments. Hear how Varèse follows no melody, but places blocks of sound next to and after one another.

artiest/edith-piaf.text:
Édith Piaf, born Édith Giovanna Gassion in 1915 in Paris, is regarded as the greatest singer of France. Her mother, a singer and circus performer, left her at birth. Her father, an acrobat from Normandy, went off to war in 1916, and Édith grew up with her grandmother in a brothel in Bernay, where the women looked after her. At fourteen she began touring with her father. In 1935 the nightclub owner Louis Leplée discovered her in Paris.

During the German occupation her fame grew, and in 1945 she wrote the lyrics of La Vie en rose, her best-known song. In the late 1940s she was the most popular performer in France. She toured Europe, South America and the United States, where she appeared eight times on The Ed Sullivan Show. Among her greatest songs are L'Accordéoniste from 1940, Hymne à l'amour from 1949, Padam, padam from 1951, La Foule from 1957, Milord from 1959 and Non, je ne regrette rien from 1960. Until a few months before her death in 1963 she gave concerts, including runs at the Paris Olympia. Her last song, L'Homme de Berlin, she recorded in April 1963 with her husband Théo Sarapo.

Piaf sang chanson réaliste and ballads about love, loss and sorrow, often autobiographical. Her voice is powerful and tremulous, accompanied by accordion and orchestra. For the French she has become a symbol of their own culture, and her life formed the basis of several films, including La Vie en Rose from 2007.
artiest/edith-piaf.listen: Listen to La vie en rose and notice how Piaf, with her tremulous voice, lets the phrases slowly unfold. Which instruments accompany her, and what atmosphere does that evoke?

artiest/edmund-meisel.text: Edmund Meisel was born in Vienna in 1894 and worked in Berlin as a violinist and conductor. In 1926 he wrote, in a short time, the music for the German premiere of Eisenstein's Panzerkreuzer Potemkin. He followed the rapid montage with hard rhythms, repeated motifs and dissonances, like a machine that keeps going faster. The audience reacted fiercely, and the music contributed to the political uproar around the film. For Walter Ruttmann's Berlin: Die Sinfonie der Großstadt (1927) he made a score full of city noises, train rhythms and jazz. He then also worked on Eisenstein's Oktjabr (1928). Meisel died in 1930, aged 36, just as sound film broke through.
artiest/edmund-meisel.listen: Notice the mechanical repetition: short motifs are repeated ever faster and louder, just like the montage on screen.

artiest/edvard-grieg.text: Edvard Grieg came from Bergen, studied in Leipzig and then sought a Norwegian voice of his own, nourished by the folk music of his country. His Piano Concerto in A minor from 1868 brought him international success, and Liszt sight-read it in Rome. For Henrik Ibsen's Peer Gynt he wrote incidental music, from which In the Hall of the Mountain King became world famous. That piece repeats a single short theme, ever faster and louder.
artiest/edvard-grieg.listen: Listen to In the Hall of the Mountain King and hear how a single short theme begins softly in the low instruments and becomes ever faster and louder.

artiest/edward-b-powell.text:
Edward Benson Powell was an American arranger, orchestrator and composer, born in 1909 in Savanna, Illinois. He began as a self-taught arranger for a dance band at school and in this way attracted the attention of the jazz musician Fletcher Henderson. In the early 1930s he worked as an orchestrator on Broadway for Harms-Chappell, where he met colleagues who, like him, later moved to Hollywood. There, in the early 1930s, he became an orchestrator for Alfred Newman at United Artists, and worked, among other things, on Eddie Cantor's Kid Millions.

Powell remained Newman's right-hand man at 20th Century Fox for more than thirty years and contributed to the music of around four hundred films. In 1936 he recommended David Raksin, and together they arranged Charlie Chaplin's music for Modern Times. On The Goldwyn Follies of 1938 he made the arrangements of George Gershwin's last songs, Love Is Here to Stay and Love Walked In. Together with Robert Russell Bennett and Conrad Salinger he orchestrated Newman's music for Gunga Din. He also worked on the score of The Song of Bernadette from 1943 and on the film versions of the Rodgers and Hammerstein musicals. In 1946 and 1947 he was president of the American Society of Music Arrangers.

To the public his name often remained invisible. Yet he was one of the arrangers who defined the recognisable sound of the great Hollywood studios, the full, colourful orchestra of classic film music. His fellow composer Oscar Levant counted him among the great specialists of the trade. He died in 1984.
artiest/edward-b-powell.listen: Listen to the music of Charlie Chaplin's Modern Times and notice how the orchestra follows the images, from soft to exuberant. Can you hear how the arranger colours a melody with different instruments each time?

artiest/edward-vesala.text:
Edward Vesala, born Martti Vesala, was a Finnish drummer and composer from avant-garde jazz. He was born in 1945 in Mäntyharju and in the 1960s began playing in jazz and rock bands such as Blues Section and Apollo. In 1969 his album Souljumppaa was released. In the 1970s he led jazz groups of his own, including a quartet with the Polish trumpeter Tomasz Stańko and the saxophonist Tomasz Szukalski. He also played in Toto Blanke's Electric Circus and recorded with the Norwegian saxophonist Jan Garbarek. Albums from this period include Nan Madol from 1974, Satu from 1977 and Open from 1979.

In the 1980s and 1990s he made several albums with his own compositions and with his group Sound & Fury, an ensemble of about ten players, mostly his students. Its members included the saxophonists Jorma Tapio and Pepa Päivinen, the guitarists Raoul Björkenheim and Jimi Sumén, and the harpist and keyboardist Iro Haarla, his wife. Their music combined jazz with classical music, tango and folk music.

Vesala was the most important drummer in Finnish jazz, and he brought that scene into contact with Polish and Norwegian jazz. His drumming was that of a composer: he gave the percussion a melodic role instead of merely a rhythmic one. He died in 1999 in Yläne, aged 54.
artiest/edward-vesala.listen: Listen to Nan Madol by Edward Vesala and notice how the drums not only make the music swing but also colour it. Can you hear how percussion here almost becomes melody?

artiest/eelco-gelling.text:
Eelco Gelling was born in 1946 in Zwartsluis. In the early 1960s he played guitar in The Rocking Hurricanes and The Rocking Strings, small groups that played guitar music in the style of The Shadows. Around 1964 the singer Harry Muskee joined. The repertoire became more bluesy and the band carried on as Cuby + Blizzards, with a first single in 1965 and a series of albums from 1966.

Cuby + Blizzards became well known in the Netherlands, Germany and England. The band played and recorded with the American bluesman Eddie Boyd and toured with Van Morrison and John Mayall. Mayall asked Gelling to join his Bluesbreakers, as Peter Green's successor, but Gelling stayed with his own band. The album Appleknockers Flophouse (1969) is regarded as one of the best Dutch blues records, and his guitar playing is compared with that of Eric Clapton, Peter Green and Mick Taylor. He played a 1960 Gibson Les Paul, which he continued to use for years.

In 1976 Gelling became a member of Golden Earring. On the album Contraband his slide guitar stands out, and he plays on Golden Earring Live. During an American tour he quit, after disagreement over the musical direction and after his Les Paul was stolen from a taxi in New York. Afterwards he played in, among others, the Muskee Gang and his own Eelco Gelling Band. In 2015 he was inducted into the Dutch Blues Hall of Fame. His raw, heavy blues playing showed that Dutch musicians could take the blues just as seriously as their English contemporaries.
artiest/eelco-gelling.listen: Listen to a track from Appleknockers Flophouse by Cuby + Blizzards and notice Gelling's guitar. Hear how his playing matches that of English blues guitarists such as Eric Clapton and Peter Green.

artiest/ehnes-quartet.text:
The Ehnes Quartet is a string quartet built around the Canadian-American violinist James Ehnes. Ehnes was born in 1976 in Brandon, Manitoba, the son of a trumpet teacher and a former ballet dancer. He began violin lessons as a child and was already touring with Jeunesses Musicales Canada at sixteen. He has performed as a soloist with major orchestras in North America and Europe, such as the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra and the London orchestras, and plays the 1715 Stradivarius known as the ex-Marsick. He is artistic director of the Seattle Chamber Music Society.

In the quartet Ehnes plays together with the violinist Amy Schwartz Moretti, the violist Che-Yen Chen and the cellist Edward Arron. Their recordings include Schubert's String Quartet No. 14, Death and the Maiden, together with Sibelius's Intimate Voices, from 2016, and the late string quartets of Beethoven, released in 2021 and 2022. An album of American chamber music has also appeared. Ehnes's recordings have won many prizes, including Grammys, Junos and Gramophone Awards.

The quartet shows what the string quartets of Beethoven and Schubert have to offer in a contemporary, clear performance, with four string players who play as one instrument.
artiest/ehnes-quartet.listen: Listen to the opening of Schubert's Death and the Maiden and notice how the four strings begin together at first, almost like a chorale. Can you hear how the voices then each take on a role of their own?

artiest/einsturzende-neubauten.text:
Einstürzende Neubauten are an experimental group from West Berlin. The name means collapsing new buildings. The first performance was on 1 April 1980 at the Moon Club, with, among others, Blixa Bargeld and N.U. Unruh, who would remain the core of the band. In 1981 the fifteen-year-old Alexander Hacke and the percussionist F.M. Einheit joined, and shortly afterwards the bassist Mark Chung. That line-up lasted almost fifteen years.

The debut album Kollaps (1981) blended raw punk with industrial noise. The band built instruments of their own from scrap metal and played on metal sheets, tools and building materials. On the early records Bargeld screams above a racket of hitting and scraping. The performances were notorious: in 1984 a concert in London was stopped when the band went through the stage with drills and pneumatic drills. With Halber Mensch (1985) the music gained more structure, and Bargeld moved from screaming to poetic singing. Fünf auf der nach oben offenen Richterskala (1987) and Haus der Lüge (1989) were also successful in the United States and Japan.

From Tabula Rasa (1993) the sound became softer and more electronic. Meanwhile, until 2003, Bargeld also played guitar in Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds. Einstürzende Neubauten showed that noise and materials from the building site can be music, and thus became one of the most important groups in industrial music.
artiest/einsturzende-neubauten.listen: Listen to Yü-Gung (Fütter mein Ego) and try to recognise the sounds: which sound like metal or tools and which like ordinary instruments? Also notice how the rhythm keeps repeating.

artiest/eiv-r.text:
Eivør Pálsdóttir, Eivør for short, is a Faroese singer and songwriter, born in 1983 and raised in Syðrugøta. She appeared on television at the age of thirteen. In 1999, aged fifteen, she became the singer of the group Clickhaze, and a year later her first album, Eivør Pálsdóttir, was released. In 2002 she moved to Reykjavik to study music. In 2004 she was named Faroese of the Year. She made albums such as Krákan from 2003, Trøllabundin from 2005 and Mannabarn from 2007, which was released simultaneously in an English version, Human Child.

With Larva from 2010 she left her folk sound for a more experimental and more electronic style. Room from 2012 won three Faroese music awards, including best album. In 2015 the two sister albums Bridges in English and Slør in Faroese were released. In 2016 she worked with Bear McCreary on the music for the computer game God of War and performed it live with an orchestra. That year At the Heart of a Selkie with the DR Big Band also appeared. In 2018 came a collaboration with John Lunn for a television series. Later she signed to Season of Mist and in 2025 to Nuclear Blast.

Eivør combines Nordic folk, jazz, pop and electronics, often with heavy, rhythmic singing and mythical subjects. Her voice is powerful and can sound both whisper-soft and raw. She brings the music of the Faroe Islands to an international audience, and shows how tradition and electronics can strengthen each other.
artiest/eiv-r.listen: Listen to a song by Eivør on the album Trøllabundin and notice her voice, which moves from soft and close to broad and powerful. Can you hear how the Faroese language shapes the rhythm of the song?

artiest/eivind-aarset.text:
Eivind Aarset is a Norwegian guitarist and composer, born in 1961. His style is associated with nu jazz and electronic music, and he often processes his guitar with many effects. Besides his own work as a bandleader he played with Ray Charles, Dee Dee Bridgewater, Ute Lemper, Ketil Bjørnstad, Andy Sheppard, Arild Andersen and Nils Petter Molvær. He also worked with Bill Laswell, Jon Hassell, Jan Garbarek, David Sylvian and Marilyn Mazur. According to the source, he recorded more than 150 albums with other artists.

His debut album Électronique Noire from 1998 was described by the New York Times as one of the best electro-jazz albums since Miles Davis. Light Extracts in 2001, Connected in 2004 and Sonic Codex in 2007 followed, among others, all for the label Jazzland. In 2012 he made Dream Logic for ECM, with Jan Bang and Erik Honoré for production and sound design. At the Punkt Festival in Kristiansand in 2013 he played with Arve Henriksen, Jan Bang, Erik Honoré and Ingar Zach, and his Dream Logic concert appeared on a list of the best live shows of that year.

Aarset often uses the guitar not as a solo instrument but as a source of sound and space, processed with electronics and loops. He belongs to the generation of Norwegian musicians who linked jazz and electronics, and showed that in modern jazz a guitar can also serve as a plane of sound.
artiest/eivind-aarset.listen: Listen to Dream Logic and notice how the guitar barely sounds like a guitar, but like a floating plane of sound. Can you hear the effects that stretch the notes and let them die away?

artiest/ekseption.text:
Ekseption was a Dutch rock band that existed from 1967 to 1989 and played mainly instrumental progressive rock and classical rock. The pivot of the changing line-up was Rein van den Broek, a conservatoire-trained trumpeter and the only musician who played on all the albums. The group grew out of the secondary-school band The Jokers, which Van den Broek had founded in 1958. At first it was called The Incrowd, after the Ramsey Lewis tune, but when it turned out that the name was already taken, it became Ekseption in 1967.

Initially the group played jazz, pop and R&B covers. In 1969, shortly after the keyboardist Rick van der Linden had joined, the band saw The Nice live and Van der Linden decided to concentrate on classical rock arrangements. With these Ekseption had success in the 1970s, with Dutch top ten singles of arrangements of Beethoven's Fifth and Bach's Air. Van der Linden took over the leadership, as he himself said in a press release around the album Ekseption 5. After the album Trinity in 1973 his bandmates asked him to leave. He founded Trace, and his successor Hans Jansen gave Ekseption a more jazz-oriented direction.

Ekseption shows how pop and classical music found each other in the 1960s and 1970s. The group placed Beethoven and Bach in a setting with drums, organ and horns, and so reached an audience that might not have sought out the classical pieces themselves. The 5th is their arrangement of Beethoven.
artiest/ekseption.listen: Listen to The 5th and notice how Beethoven's familiar four notes are taken up by organ and horns, with a solid drum rhythm underneath. What do you hear that would not be there in Beethoven himself?

artiest/electric-light-orchestra.text:
Electric Light Orchestra, ELO for short, is an English rock band from Birmingham, formed in 1970 by the multi-instrumentalists Jeff Lynne and Roy Wood and the drummer Bev Bevan. The name is a pun on electric light and light orchestral music, the BBC's light orchestral programming. Wood, who had previously played in The Move, wanted to make rock music with violins, cellos and horns, so that rock would carry on where the Beatles had stopped. On 12 July 1970 he added cellos to a song by Lynne, and 10538 Overture became the group's first song.

After Wood's departure in 1972 Lynne became the sole leader. The group made albums such as The Electric Light Orchestra in 1971, On the Third Day in 1973 and Eldorado from 1974, and later Face the Music, A New World Record, Out of the Blue and Discovery. Hits included Roll Over Beethoven, Livin' Thing, Telephone Line, Mr. Blue Sky and Do Ya. In 1986 Lynne disbanded the group. Between 1972 and 1986 ELO had 27 songs in the British top 40, and sold more than 50 million records.

The music combines smooth pop songs with strings and with a futuristic atmosphere in the sleeves and the show. The sound is full and layered, with choruses, strings and a solid rhythm. ELO showed that classical arrangements and rock could go together in robust, melodic pop music.
artiest/electric-light-orchestra.listen: Listen to Mr. Blue Sky and notice how the strings, the backing vocals and the rhythm section together make a full sound. Can you hear how the melody is taken over by a different part of the orchestra each time?

artiest/electric-youth.text:
Electric Youth is a Canadian synth-pop duo from Toronto. The singer and songwriter Bronwyn Griffin and the producer, songwriter, synthesizer player and drummer Austin Garrick have been together since Grade 8. Their breakthrough came in 2011 with A Real Hero, in collaboration with College, which was given a prominent place in the film Drive. Garrick wrote the song partly about Chesley Sullenberger and the emergency landing of flight 1549. Spin magazine named A Real Hero one of the twenty best songs of 2011.

In 2013 the duo signed to Last Gang Records and Secretly Canadian. Their debut album Innerworld was released in 2014. Rolling Stone named them in 2014 one of the ten artists you needed to know, and that autumn their first tour of the United States and Canada followed. They then made Breathing, the music for a lost film, in 2017, the album Memory Emotion in 2019, which received a Juno nomination, and music for the films Come True in 2021 and North of Normal in 2025.

Their music uses synthesizers and drum machines from the 1980s, with soft, almost whispered singing. Garrick says that they do not want to imitate the past and would rather make things for the future. The duo shows how the sound of synth-pop is returning in film music and playlists, as an atmosphere full of nostalgia and at the same time as a new sound.
artiest/electric-youth.listen: Listen to A Real Hero and notice Bronwyn Griffin's soft voice above the glowing synthesizers. Can you hear how calm the rhythm stays, while the chorus still sounds grand?

artiest/eleni-karaindrou.text: Eleni Karaindrou studied piano and music theory in Athens and ethnomusicology in Paris. From Taxidi sta Kythira (1984) she wrote the music for all of Theo Angelopoulos's films, until his death in 2012. Her music is slow, austere and melancholic. She uses small ensembles: strings, oboe, clarinet, accordion, harp or viola, often alongside Greek folk instruments. Long, repeated melodies suit Angelopoulos's long shots. Her soundtracks were released on the label ECM, which issued them as albums in their own right. For To vlemma tou Odyssea (1995) the violist Kim Kashkashian plays the leading role. Mia aioniotita kai mia mera (1998) won the Palme d'Or at Cannes.
artiest/eleni-karaindrou.listen: Notice the slow, repeated melody on a solo instrument such as oboe or viola, above a quietly sustained accompaniment.

artiest/elis-regina.text:
Elis Regina Carvalho Costa, known as Elis Regina, was a Brazilian singer of bossa nova, MPB and jazz. She was born in 1945 in Porto Alegre and began as a child on the radio programme Clube de Guri. In her early teens she signed a record contract and a few years later travelled to Rio de Janeiro, where she recorded her first album. Her first albums included Viva a Brotolândia from 1961 and Poema de amor from 1962. Shortly before the military coup of 1964 she moved to Rio permanently.

In 1965 she became known throughout Brazil through her performance of Arrastão, a song by Edu Lobo and Vinícius de Moraes, at the first song festival of TV Excelsior. Soon afterwards she became a regular guest on the television programme O Fino da Bossa on TV Record. She was known for her vocals, her interpretation and her stage presence, and was given the nicknames Hurricane and Little Pepper. In Europe she criticised the regime during a tour, and her popularity protected her, although she was later threatened with imprisonment. She later made albums such as Elis from 1966, Elis especial from 1968 and Como & porque from 1969. She had children with Ronaldo Bôscoli and with Cesar Camargo Mariano, and her daughter Maria Rita and son Pedro Mariano became singers themselves.

Elis Regina died in 1982 at the age of 36, which shocked Brazil. A musical wake at the Teatro Bandeirantes in São Paulo drew more than fifteen thousand fans. Her name stands for a voice of almost unlimited power and feeling, and for the way Brazilian popular music acquired a character of its own in the 1960s and 1970s.
artiest/elis-regina.listen: Listen to Arrastão by Elis Regina and notice the fierce, almost spoken force with which she begins the song. Can you hear how she opens up in the chorus and how big her voice then sounds?

artiest/elis-regina-en-antonio-carlos-jo.text:
Elis Regina was born in 1945 in Porto Alegre and began as a child on the radio programme Clube de Guri. At fifteen she signed a record contract and a few years later travelled to Rio de Janeiro, where she recorded her first album. She sang bossa nova, MPB and jazz. In 1965 she won a song contest on television with Arrastão by Edu Lobo and Vinícius de Moraes, and became the best-selling Brazilian artist since Carmen Miranda. She was given a regular slot on the television programme O Fino da Bossa.

Elis was known for her vocalisation and for her interpretations and performances. She was given the nicknames Hurricane and Little Pepper. During the military dictatorship she criticised the regime on tour in Europe, and she was threatened with imprisonment if she did not sing the national anthem. Her well-known recordings include Como Nossos Pais, Upa Neguinho, Madalena and Casa no Campo. She died in 1982 at the age of thirty-six, which shocked the whole of Brazil.

In the 1970s she recorded Elis and Tom with Antônio Carlos Jobim, the composer who had made a great name in bossa nova. On it is Águas de Março, a song by Jobim in which the lyrics set down image after image like a list. Elis's singing gives it energy and playfulness, alongside the calm, jazzy accompaniment. The recording is regarded as a high point of Brazilian popular music.
artiest/elis-regina-en-antonio-carlos-jo.listen: Listen to Águas de Março and notice how the two voices alternate and roll the lyrics along like a string of images. How does the simple accompaniment keep the song moving?

artiest/elisabeth-lutyens.text: Elisabeth Lutyens, daughter of the architect Edwin Lutyens, was one of the first British composers to use the twelve-tone technique. She had few opportunities in concert life, so she earned her living from film and radio. In the 1960s she wrote horror music for Hammer, such as Paranoiac (1963), and for their rival Amicus, such as Dr. Terror's House of Horrors (1965) and The Skull (1965). Her modern language suited fear and unease well: atonal lines, harsh clusters, unusual tone colours and little recognisable melody. For a long time these scores were unreleased. Only recently have they appeared on CD.
artiest/elisabeth-lutyens.listen: Notice the absence of a fixed key: atonal lines and sharp chords create unease instead of a melody to remember.

artiest/elizabeth-lutyens.text:
Elisabeth Lutyens was born in London in 1906, the daughter of the famous architect Sir Edwin Lutyens and Lady Emily Bulwer-Lytton. At the age of nine she already wanted to become a composer. In 1922 she studied in Paris at the École Normale de Musique, in 1923 she travelled to India with her mother, and from 1926 to 1930 she studied at the Royal College of Music in London. She later married Edward Clark, a conductor and former BBC producer who had studied with Schoenberg. She often wrote her music in great seclusion, alongside the care of her children.

Her success came in 1947 with a cantata on Rimbaud's poem Ô saisons, Ô châteaux. The BBC at first refused to perform it because the soprano part was supposedly too high, but was afterwards the organisation that gave the first performances of much of her work from the 1940s and 1950s. Later she wrote Quincunx for orchestra with soprano and baritone, which was premiered in 1962 at the Cheltenham Music Festival. She claimed that she had invented serialism independently before she had seen so much as a note of Webern.

To pay the bills Lutyens wrote film music for the horror films of Hammer and Amicus Productions. She was the first British woman to score a feature film, with Penny and the Pownall Case from 1948. In her film work the modern, angular music of the avant-garde can be heard, and she therefore shows that that style also found its way into the cinema in the 1960s. In 1972 her autobiography A Goldfish Bowl was published. She died in 1983.
artiest/elizabeth-lutyens.listen: Listen to Main Title and notice the sharp, angular sounds of the orchestra and the threatening atmosphere. How does such modern, atonal music suit a horror film?

artiest/elizeth-cardoso.text:
Elizeth Cardoso was a Brazilian singer and actress, born in 1920 in Rio de Janeiro. Her father was a serenade singer who played guitar, her mother sang as an amateur. Between 1930 and 1935 she worked, among other things, as a shop assistant and hairdresser. On her sixteenth birthday she was discovered by Jacob do Bandolim. Because she earned little, in 1939 she began performing in clubs and cinemas, and her success grew quickly. In 1950, with the support of Ataulfo Alves, she recorded songs such as Braços vazios and Mensageiro da saudade.

In 1958 Vinicius de Moraes asked her to sing on an album of songs by himself and Tom Jobim. That album, Canção do Amor Demais, is regarded as the first bossa nova album and was the beginning of the new genre. Cardoso herself was not considered primarily a bossa nova singer. She afterwards made many more albums, including Canções à meia luz from 1955, Noturno from 1957, Magnífica and Naturalmente from 1959, and in total recorded more than forty albums in Brazil, Portugal and other countries. Her career lasted almost seven decades. She died of cancer in 1990.

The foundation of her work remained samba, which she sang with great feeling. She sang in many styles, but her voice stayed warm and precise. With Canção do Amor Demais she kicked off a musical movement that would be played all over the world. In 2021 Google marked her hundred-and-first birthday with a Doodle.
artiest/elizeth-cardoso.listen: Listen to a song from Canção do Amor Demais and notice how her voice stays soft and clear above the guitar accompaniment. Can you hear how little accompaniment is needed?

artiest/ella-fitzgerald.text: Ella Fitzgerald won a talent contest at the Apollo Theater in Harlem as a teenager in 1934. The drummer Chick Webb took her into his orchestra at the Savoy Ballroom, and in 1938 they had a big hit with A-Tisket, A-Tasket. Like many singers she had Louis Armstrong as an example; later she made three albums with him. In the 1940s she took over the language of bebop in her scat singing. For Norman Granz and his label Verve she recorded, from 1956, the songbooks of songs by the great American composers. On Ella in Berlin (1960) she forgot the words of Mack the Knife and improvised new ones.
artiest/ella-fitzgerald.listen: Listen to the scat: she sings like a horn player, with fast lines and quotations from other songs.

artiest/ellie-goulding.text:
Ellie Goulding is an English singer-songwriter, born in 1986 in Hereford and raised in the village of Lyonshall in Herefordshire, in a poor family. She played the clarinet from the age of nine, learned the guitar at fourteen and was already writing songs at fifteen. In 2009 she was discovered by the manager Jamie Lillywhite and signed to Polydor Records. Her first single Under the Sheets was released through the independent label Neon Gold, and in December the EP An Introduction to Ellie Goulding followed.

Her debut album Lights from 2010 went to the top of the British album chart, with three successful singles: a cover of Elton John's Your Song, Starry Eyed and Lights. Halcyon from 2012 began with the single Anything Could Happen, and the reissue Halcyon Days of 2013 brought Burn, her first number one in England. Delirium followed in 2015, Brightest Blue in 2020 and Higher Than Heaven in 2023. Between 2016 and 2020 she took a break because of an anxiety disorder and press attention. She won two Brit Awards and is also active in the environmental movement.

Goulding combines a light, almost quivering voice with electronic pop music and dance beats. She brings together the sound of acoustic singer-songwriters and dance-floor production, and so fits into the wave of British pop of the 2010s, in which electronics and folk ran into one another.
artiest/ellie-goulding.listen: Listen to Lights and notice the light, high voice above the electronic sounds. Can you hear how the song builds towards a chorus that consists mainly of layers of synthesizers?

artiest/ellie-greenwich.text:
Ellie Greenwich was born in 1940 in Brooklyn, New York, and at the age of ten moved with her parents to Levittown. She learned to play the accordion and was already writing songs as a teenager. At seventeen she recorded her first single of her own for RCA. In 1959 she met Jeff Barry, who would become her husband and most important writing partner. In 1962 Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller gave her a contract as a staff songwriter. She also sang so many demos that she was known in New York as the Demo Queen.

In 1962 Greenwich and Barry married, and from then on they wrote only with each other. Together with the producer Phil Spector they made Be My Baby and Baby, I Love You for The Ronettes, Then He Kissed Me and Da Doo Ron Ron for The Crystals and Christmas (Baby Please Come Home) for Darlene Love. Do Wah Diddy Diddy became a number 1 hit for Manfred Mann in 1964, and at the label Red Bird they wrote Chapel of Love for The Dixie Cups and Leader of the Pack. As The Raindrops they also recorded records themselves, with Greenwich singing all the female voices.

Their songs are short, cheerful and instantly memorable, with choruses full of sounds such as da doo ron ron. In 2015 Rolling Stone placed Greenwich and Barry nineteenth on its list of the best songwriters of all time. After their divorce in 1965 they still produced the young Neil Diamond together. River Deep, Mountain High for Ike & Tina Turner was their last work with Phil Spector. In 1985 the musical Leader of the Pack, about her life, opened on Broadway. Greenwich died in 2009.
artiest/ellie-greenwich.listen: Listen to Da Doo Ron Ron by The Crystals and notice the chorus: the nonsense words of the title become a hook that you sing along to at once. Also hear how short and simply the song is built.

artiest/ellie-mannette.text:
Elliott Anthony Mannette, known as Ellie Mannette, was a Trinidadian instrument maker and steelpan player, born in 1927 in Sans Souci in Trinidad. He is called the father of the modern steel drum. As a child he became fascinated by metal and tools, and at eleven he was already playing in Alexander's Ragtime Band. From the mid-1930s he was involved in the development of resonant steel. In 1948 he was offered a scholarship to study music in London, which he turned down in order to be able to build more pans.

In 1951 the Trinidad All Steel Percussion Orchestra, TASPO, travelled to Britain to show the new instrument at the Festival of Britain. Mannette was a member and tuner of that orchestra. In the early 1960s he built up the navy's steel band in the United States, and then in New York built instruments for a youth project. From 1967 he founded hundreds of steel bands, mainly at colleges and universities. In 1991 West Virginia University invited him to teach students to build and play pans, and that remained his workplace. He died in Morgantown in 2018.

Mannette devised important innovations: he was the first to use a 55-gallon oil drum instead of biscuit tins or soapboxes, and pressed the top of the drum into a hollow shape, so that there was more room for notes. In this way the steelpan became an instrument that could be played all over the world. His work hangs in museums, including the Smithsonian.
artiest/ellie-mannette.listen: Listen to a steel band recording from Trinidad and notice the bright, ringing sound of the pans. Can you hear that the different pans each get a role of their own, from melody to bass?

artiest/elliott-smith.text:
Elliott Smith, born Steven Paul Smith, was an American musician and singer-songwriter. He was born in 1969 in Omaha and grew up mainly in Texas, and lived a large part of his life in Portland, Oregon, where he became known in the 1990s. He began playing piano at nine and guitar at ten. At fourteen he moved to his father in Portland. There he began calling himself Elliott, and played for years in the rock band Heatmiser.

In 1994 his solo career began, with records for the independent labels Cavity Search and Kill Rock Stars, such as Roman Candle and the self-titled Elliott Smith from 1995. Either/Or was released in 1997. That year he signed to DreamWorks, for which he recorded XO from 1998 and Figure 8 from 2000. His song Miss Misery, recorded for the film Good Will Hunting, was nominated for an Oscar for Best Original Song. From a Basement on the Hill was released in 2004, after his death. He died in 2003 in Los Angeles. His struggle with alcohol, drugs and depression often recurred in his lyrics.

His music is quiet and intimate: a soft, double-tracked voice, acoustic guitar or piano, and later fuller arrangements with strings and drums. Smith showed how sorrow and vulnerability can sound in a modest folk song, and thereby became an example for many later singer-songwriters.
artiest/elliott-smith.listen: Listen to Miss Misery and notice the soft, double-tracked voice above the guitar. Can you hear how quiet the song is, even when the band comes in?

artiest/ellis-marsalis.text:
Ellis Marsalis Jr. was an American jazz pianist and teacher, born in 1934 in New Orleans. His father was a businessman and activist. At secondary school he played tenor saxophone and piano, and performed with an R&B band. He then served a year in the Marine Corps, mainly as a pianist, and studied at Dillard University. In the 1950s and 1960s he played with Ed Blackwell, Cannonball Adderley, Nat Adderley and Al Hirt. In the 1970s he taught at the New Orleans Center for Creative Arts.

His students included Terence Blanchard, Harry Connick Jr. and Donald Harrison. He made almost twenty albums of his own, such as Friends and Solo Piano from 1991, Heart of Gold from 1992, Whistle Stop from 1994 and A Night at Snug Harbor, New Orleans from 1995. He also played on records by David Fathead Newman, Eddie Harris, Marcus Roberts and Courtney Pine. In the 1980s and 1990s he received more attention as the head of the Marsalis family, when his sons Branford and Wynton became famous jazz musicians. With his wife Dolores he had six sons, of whom Delfeayo and Jason also became jazz musicians. In 2011 he and his sons together received the NEA Jazz Masters Award.

As a teacher he said: we don't learn jazz, we learn music. He encouraged students to get to know the history and at the same time to make their own discoveries. In this way he gave New Orleans a new generation of jazz musicians. He was inducted into the Louisiana Music Hall of Fame in 2008, died in 2020 and in 2023 received a posthumous Grammy Trustees Award.
artiest/ellis-marsalis.listen: Listen to a recording of Ellis Marsalis on piano and notice how he leaves a lot of space with few notes. Can you hear the light, bluesy touch in his playing?

artiest/elmer-bernstein.text: Elmer Bernstein from New York studied piano and composition, among others with Stefan Wolpe. He broke through with Otto Preminger's The Man with the Golden Arm (1955). For it he used a jazz big band to give voice to the main character's heroin addiction. That was new in Hollywood. He then wrote in many styles. The Ten Commandments (1956) is a grand biblical epic. The rhythmic, Copland-like theme of The Magnificent Seven (1960) became one of the best-known Western themes. In To Kill a Mockingbird (1962) he used, by contrast, piano, harp and flute, seen through a child's eyes. His only Oscar he won for Thoroughly Modern Millie (1967).
artiest/elmer-bernstein.listen: Compare the jazz big band of Golden Arm with the open, rhythmic Western theme and the childlike simplicity of Mockingbird.

artiest/elton-john.text:
Elton John was really called Reginald Dwight and was born in 1947 in Pinner, near London. As a small boy he played on his grandmother's piano, and at eleven he won a scholarship to the Saturday classes of the Royal Academy of Music. At fifteen he played piano in a pub, then in the blues band Bluesology. His stage name dates from that time, as does the collaboration with the lyricist Bernie Taupin, with whom he would write most of his songs.

After the debut Empty Sky (1969) he broke through in 1970 with the ballad Your Song. In the 1970s the hits followed each other quickly: Tiny Dancer, Rocket Man, Crocodile Rock, Daniel, and on the double album Goodbye Yellow Brick Road (1973) Bennie and the Jets and Candle in the Wind, among others. With Kiki Dee he sang Don't Go Breaking My Heart. In 1985 he had a big hit with Nikita, with George Michael on backing vocals. Later he wrote music for The Lion King (1994) and for musicals such as Billy Elliot.

Elton John builds his songs around the piano, which he plays with the energy of his boyhood heroes Little Richard and Jerry Lee Lewis. On stage he stood out with wild costumes and enormous glasses. He became one of the best-selling artists of all time. His new version of Candle in the Wind, recorded in 1997 after the death of Princess Diana, is the best-selling single ever. Since the late 1980s he has committed himself to the fight against AIDS.
artiest/elton-john.listen: Listen to Nikita and notice how the story of a love on the other side of the Wall is packaged in a pop song. Listen in the backing vocals for the voice of George Michael.

artiest/elvin-jones.text: Elvin Jones from Pontiac, Michigan, came from a musical family; his brothers were the pianist Hank Jones and the trumpeter Thad Jones. From 1960 to 1966 he was the drummer in John Coltrane's quartet. His playing was full and rolling: he played rhythms in three against four and let the beat, as it were, roll. With Coltrane he conducted long, intense dialogues, especially in the live pieces. After the quartet he led groups of his own, with, among others, the saxophonists Joe Farrell and Dave Liebman, and he played until shortly before his death in 2004. He often gave workshops in schools and prisons.
artiest/elvin-jones.listen: Hear the drums as waves: not a rigid beat, but a continuous movement.

artiest/elvis-costello.text:
Elvis Costello was born in London in 1954 as Declan Patrick MacManus. His father was a trumpeter and singer, his mother worked in record shops, so he grew up among music. His career began when British punk emerged. He kept his broad musical knowledge hidden at first, but it came fully to the surface later: his styles range from rhythm and blues and country to jazz, baroque pop and classical music.

His debut My Aim Is True came out in 1977. It produced no hit singles, but it does contain the ballad Alison, one of his best-known songs. The records This Year's Model (1978) and Armed Forces (1979) helped define the new wave genre. He was then playing with his band the Attractions. From late 1977 to early 1980 all his singles reached the British top thirty, with Oliver's Army in 1979 as the biggest hit. In America success remained more modest, although he scored in 1989 with Veronica.

Costello wrote lyrics full of wordplay, in the tradition of Bob Dylan and Van Morrison, but with the ferocity of punk. He worked with the Brodsky Quartet, Allen Toussaint, The Roots and Burt Bacharach, and wrote songs with Paul McCartney. His own songs have been recorded by many other artists. In the course he appears as an artist for whom a designer made the sleeves of his first records, a reminder of how important the imagery accompanying the music became in these years. In 2003 the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inducted him.
artiest/elvis-costello.listen: Listen to Alison from My Aim Is True. Notice how calm and almost restrained the singing is, while the lyrics are full of feeling and wordplay.

artiest/elvis-presley.text:
Elvis Presley was born in 1935 in Tupelo, Mississippi, and grew up in Memphis. He did not invent rock 'n' roll. The blues, the gospel, the rhythm and blues and the country from which that music was made already existed. But from 1956 Presley brought it to a large white audience, and through radio, records and television to the whole world. In doing so he became the model for the teen idol.

On 5 July 1954 he recorded That's All Right at Sam Phillips's Sun Studio in Memphis, a blues by Arthur Crudup from 1946. Guitarist Scotty Moore and bassist Bill Black played along. On the B-side was Blue Moon of Kentucky, a bluegrass song by Bill Monroe: Black blues and white country on a single record. At the end of 1955 RCA bought his contract, with Colonel Tom Parker as his manager. Heartbreak Hotel became his first number 1 hit in 1956. That same year he turned Hound Dog, previously a hit for Big Mama Thornton, into a fast rock song.

From 1958 to 1960 Presley was in military service, stationed in West Germany. Afterwards he became a singer for the whole family and starred in a string of Hollywood films. A television special in 1968 brought him back as a rock singer and led to regular concert residencies in Las Vegas. He died in 1977 at Graceland, his home in Memphis. His influence reached far: the British rockers of the 1950s took him as their example, and in 1979 The Clash borrowed the lettering of his first album for the sleeve of London Calling.
artiest/elvis-presley.listen: That's All Right was recorded without a drummer. Listen to how Bill Black's double bass carries the rhythm, while Scotty Moore plays short electric guitar lines around it and Presley himself plays acoustic rhythm guitar.

artiest/emerson-lake-en-palmer.text:
Emerson, Lake & Palmer was an English progressive rock band formed in London in 1970. The three members came from other well-known groups: the keyboardist Keith Emerson from The Nice, the singer and bassist Greg Lake from King Crimson and the drummer Carl Palmer from Atomic Rooster. They chose their three surnames as the band name, so that not all the attention would go to Emerson. After a performance at the Isle of Wight Festival in August 1970, in front of an enormous audience, they were famous at once.

The debut album Emerson, Lake & Palmer was released at the end of 1970. It contains rock arrangements of classical pieces by Bartók, Janáček and Bach, but also Lucky Man, an acoustic ballad that Lake had already written at the age of twelve. Tarkus (1971), with a title piece of twenty minutes, Pictures at an Exhibition after Mussorgsky, Trilogy (1972) and Brain Salad Surgery (1973) followed. The sound revolved around Emerson, who played Hammond organ, piano and the Moog synthesizer with great showmanship. On stage he used a large modular Moog, which sometimes went out of tune from the heat of the lights.

After Works (1977) and Love Beach (1978) the group broke up in 1979, although reunions and the albums Black Moon (1992) and In the Hot Seat (1994) followed later. Emerson and Lake both died in 2016. ELP was one of the most popular prog rock bands of the 1970s and showed that the synthesizer could be a solo instrument, just as loud and conspicuous as the electric guitar.
artiest/emerson-lake-en-palmer.listen: Listen to Lucky Man and notice the difference between the beginning, with acoustic guitar and vocals, and the ending. There the Moog synthesizer takes over with a gliding, buzzing solo.

artiest/emil-newman.text:
Emil Newman was an American musical director and conductor who worked on more than two hundred films and television series. He was born in 1911 in Connecticut and entered films in 1940 as musical director of thirteen films. In 1941 he was credited on twenty-five titles, in 1942 on twenty-eight, and in 1943 on fifteen. His first contribution as a composer, uncredited, was Whispering Ghosts in 1942. He was nominated for an Oscar for his musical direction of Sun Valley Serenade from 1941.

Newman belonged to a well-known film family. His older brother was the composer Alfred Newman, whose children Maria, David and Thomas are also composers. His younger brother Lionel Newman was likewise a well-known film composer, and his grandson Joey Newman writes film and television music. As a result the Newman family is the most nominated extended family in the history of the Oscars. Emil himself married the supporting actress Eva May Hoffman and had two children. He died in 1984 in Woodland Hills and is buried at Forest Lawn in Glendale. Albums of his work include Sands of Iwo Jima and Island in the Sky.

His work shows how in the era of the great studios the conducting and directing of film music was a craft that was rarely in the foreground. It is the work of someone who brings the music together, so that composers, arrangers and orchestra can carry a film together.
artiest/emil-newman.listen: Listen to Sun Valley Serenade and notice how a big band and the film orchestra together set the mood. Can you hear how the music follows the movements of the dancers?

artiest/eminem.text:
Eminem is the stage name of Marshall Mathers, born in 1972 in St. Joseph, Missouri. He moved around a lot as a child, until he ended up in Detroit with his mother, in a working-class neighbourhood with mainly Black residents. There he learned to rap in freestyle battles and at open mics, such as at the Hip-Hop Shop on West 7 Mile Road. His first album, Infinite (1996), flopped. A year later he came second at the Rap Olympics in Los Angeles. His Slim Shady EP reached Jimmy Iovine of Interscope, who played the tape to Dr. Dre. He wanted to sign him immediately, even though the people around him considered a white rapper a risk.

With Dr. Dre as producer, Eminem broke through with The Slim Shady LP (1999). The Marshall Mathers LP (2000) sold 1.76 million copies in its first week in the United States, and The Eminem Show (2002) became the best-selling album in the world of that year. His lyrics were coarse and violent and caused a great deal of controversy, but also produced narrative songs such as Stan. In 2002 he played a version of himself in the film 8 Mile. The song Lose Yourself spent twelve weeks at number 1 in America and became the first hip hop song to win an Oscar.

Eminem raps fast and often rhymes on several syllables at once, a technique he practised as a teenager by pulling words apart on paper. With estimated sales of more than 220 million records he is the best-selling rapper ever. He brought hip hop to an audience of white young people in the American middle class and showed that a white rapper could be taken seriously in a Black musical culture. In 2022 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, with Dr. Dre as presenter.
artiest/eminem.listen: In Lose Yourself, listen to the structure: the song begins with spoken words over a few quiet chords, after which beat and guitar come in. In the verses, notice how the rhymes fall on two or three syllables at once.

artiest/emma-bunton.text:
Emma Bunton was born in 1976 in Finchley, in north London. She attended the Sylvia Young Theatre School and as a teenager played small roles in television series such as EastEnders and The Bill. Soon afterwards she joined a new girl group, put together from auditions after an advertisement in the trade paper The Stage in 1994. She took the place of a singer who had quickly dropped out and was the youngest of the five. The press gave her the nickname Baby Spice.

The Spice Girls signed to Virgin Records in 1995. Their first single, Wannabe (1996), spent seven weeks at number 1 in England and reached number one in thirty-four other countries, including the United States. Eight more number 1 hits followed from the albums Spice, Spiceworld and Forever. With more than a hundred million records sold, the Spice Girls are the most successful girl group ever.

After the group Bunton began a solo career. Her first single, What Took You So Long? (2001), entered at number 1 in England straight away, and the album A Girl Like Me (2001) reached number four. On Free Me (2004) and Life in Mono (2006) she chose a sound that harked back to the 1960s, to Motown and to French pop. Her version of Downtown, the hit by Petula Clark, became a charity single for Children in Need in 2006. Afterwards she worked mainly as a judge on talent shows and as a radio presenter. Bunton shows how a pop group conceived as a concept nevertheless produced five personalities of their own that the public could tell apart.
artiest/emma-bunton.listen: In Wannabe, listen to how the five voices alternate: half-rapped lines, sung passages and a chorus that they deliver together. Try to pick out Bunton's light, high voice.

artiest/emma-kirkby.text:
Dame Emma Kirkby is an English soprano and early music specialist, born in 1949. She went to school in Dorset and studied classics at Somerville College, Oxford. Her father was an officer in the Royal Navy. She had not planned to become a professional singer. At the end of the 1960s she sang in Oxford in the Schola Cantorum, a student choir led by Andrew Parrott. After her studies she became a teacher, but she became more and more involved in singing early music. For years she taught at the Dartington International Summer School and the Guildhall School of Music & Drama.

Kirkby made more than a hundred recordings: madrigals from the Italian and English Renaissance, cantatas and oratorios from the Baroque, and works by Mozart, Haydn and Johann Christian Bach. A 1981 recording with Gothic Voices of A Feather on the Breath of God, with music by Hildegard of Bingen, became well known. Later came, among others, Handel Opera Arias, Bach's wedding cantatas, Classical Kirkby with Anthony Rooley from 2002 and songs by William Byrd with Fretwork from 2005.

Her voice is clear, light and almost without vibrato, and fits the way in which early music came to be performed on period instruments in the late twentieth century. In this way she showed how Baroque music sounded before the big operatic voice became the norm. She is an example of the movement that brought early music back to the concert platform.
artiest/emma-kirkby.listen: Listen to Exsultate, jubilate by Mozart sung by Emma Kirkby and notice the clear, straight tone of her voice. Can you hear how the fast passages are sung without heavy vibrato?
